summary: Defines a URN namespace for the GSMA and a namespace-specific string for the IMEI, which identifies mobile equipment in GSM, UMTS, and LTE networks. It also covers the IMEISV. These URNs nearly always contain personal information and must be handled with care.

plainLanguage.summary: Every mobile phone has a serial number. This defines a standard way to write that number as a web-style name, and warns that it points to a person and must be handled carefully.

questions: how to write imei as urn
subtitle: A standard name for identifying mobile phones as web-addressable resources.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks identify phones by a unique 15-digit number called the IMEI, but Internet protocols need a standard format to use this identifier across systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7254 defines a URN namespace under the name 'gsma' that represents IMEIs and their variant (IMEISV, with software version) in a format compatible with web standards.
tldr.outcome: Mobile equipment can now be referred to by URNs in Internet protocols, but these URNs contain sensitive personal information and must be protected carefully.

today: RFC 7254 is an Informational RFC and remains the current specification for the GSMA IMEI URN namespace. The IANA registration is maintained by the GSMA, and the namespace is used wherever Internet protocols need to identify mobile equipment in terms compatible with cellular networks.

sections.title: Mobile Equipment and URN Naming
sections.content: The International Mobile station Equipment Identity (IMEI) is a 15-digit number permanently embedded in every mobile phone to uniquely identify that specific device. As mobile networks increasingly interwork with Internet systems, protocols need a standard way to refer to mobile equipment in formats compatible with the web. Uniform Resource Names (URNs) provide that standard format. RFC 7254 defines how to express IMEIs and IMEISVs as URNs so that Internet protocols can identify mobile devices the same way GSM, UMTS, and LTE networks do.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet uses web-style names for things. This RFC makes a web-style name you can use to point to a specific phone, based on its factory number.

sections.title: IMEI Structure and Meaning
sections.content:
An IMEI is composed of three parts. The Type Allocation Code (TAC) occupies the first 8 digits and identifies the model of the mobile equipment; the manufacturer is allocated a range of TAC values. The Serial Number (SNR) is 6 digits and uniquely identifies an individual device within that TAC. The final digit is a Spare or Check digit, always set to zero when the phone transmits its IMEI; it is used for verification in other contexts. When a phone reports its IMEI over the network, these 15 digits are transmitted in Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) format for compatibility with cellular signaling, but in the URN format they appear as plain decimal digits. The GSMA manages TAC allocation to ensure each manufacturer gets unique ranges.

The IMEISV is a 16-digit variant used to track not just the device but also its software version. It replaces the Spare digit with a 2-digit Software Version Number (SVN), allocated by the manufacturer to identify which version of the device firmware is running. This allows networks to track whether a device is running known-vulnerable software.
sections.plainLanguage: The IMEI is like your phone's serial number: 8 digits say what model it is, 6 more say which one, and 1 is a check digit. The IMEISV adds the software version on top, so you know which version the phone is running.

sections.title: URN Syntax and Format
sections.content: An IMEI URN takes the form urn:gsma:imei:tac-snr-spare, where each part is its decimal digit string. For example, urn:gsma:imei:90420156-025763-0. To represent the software version, an optional svn parameter is appended: urn:gsma:imei:90420156-025763-0;svn=42. An optional vers parameter (set to 0 or absent) indicates that the format complies with this specification; future format extensions would use a non-zero value. The GSMA manages this namespace and is responsible for any future additions to the 'gsma' NID, such as other identifiers beyond IMEI. Comparison of two IMEI URNs is case-insensitive, and the vers=0 parameter is ignored for equivalence.
sections.plainLanguage: The URN is just a way to write the three IMEI parts in a standardized order, separated by dashes. You can add a software version number at the end if you need it.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Warnings
sections.content: IMEIs are almost always personally identifiable information. Since IMEIs are easily obtained (they are visible on most phones and printed inside the battery compartment), they cannot be used as security capabilities—mere possession does not grant access. However, the RFC strongly cautions against using IMEIs for authorization, as some applications and customer service departments have inappropriately done so. The IMEISV is particularly sensitive because the software version field can expose vulnerable devices; the RFC mandates that IMEISV URNs MUST only be delivered to trusted entities within carrier networks, never to the Internet at large. IMEIs MUST NOT be included in messages intended to convey anonymity. They MUST NOT be used as user identifiers or user addresses, because phones are resold and reassigned, risking communications being misdirected to new owners. IMEIs can be used to track and identify individuals; the RFC requires that protocols carrying the IMEI URN use strongly encrypted channels (hop-by-hop at minimum, end-to-end preferred) and undergo Expert Review to ensure privacy protections are adequate.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone's ID is like your social security number: private, easily obtainable, and not for authentication. Never use it as a password. If you send it over the internet, encrypt it carefully.

sections.title: Namespace Registration and Use
sections.content: The GSMA (Global System for Mobile Communications Association), the trade association representing mobile operators worldwide, is the registrant and manager of the 'gsma' URN namespace. The namespace identifier (NID) 'gsma' was registered with IANA following RFC 3406 procedures as a formal URN namespace. The GSMA takes responsibility for maintaining uniqueness and persistence of identifiers in this namespace; once a TAC and SNR are assigned to a device, they are never reassigned. Internet users and systems may need to receive and process GSMA URNs to interoperate with GSM, UMTS, and LTE mobile devices, making the namespace's availability and standardization important. At present, the namespace is not globally resolvable (URN resolution is not defined), so it is used purely as an identifier, not as a retrievable resource locator.
sections.plainLanguage: The GSMA is in charge of this naming system. Once a phone gets an IMEI, that number stays with it for life and is never given to another phone. Internet systems just need to know how to write down these numbers.
